title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
hook: a kid on tiptoe against the height chart can't earn being taller. on the fourth line, Shankara says freedom isn't earned either

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and the third line read twice: Brahman the source of scripture, scripture the way to know Brahman. Did any sentence land two ways for you? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

At the doctor's office, a kid backs up against the height chart on the wall. The nurse reaches for the little slider. And the kid's heels start to lift. Just a bit. Maybe it'll count. Everyone in the room smiles, because everyone knows: you can stretch, you can stand up straight, but you can't earn your height. You can only find out what it is. Shankara's comment on the Brahma Sutra's fourth line makes a point a lot like that one, about the deepest thing a person can want. Freedom, he says, isn't the kind of thing you produce. Today: the line that begins with but.
screen: `HEELS LIFTING AT THE HEIGHT CHART.` → `YOU CAN'T EARN YOUR HEIGHT.` → `THE LINE THAT BEGINS WITH BUT.`

segments.voice: The fourth line says, in effect: but that, because of samanvaya, because the texts are connected in it. Samanvaya means connection: the Upanishads fit together around Brahman. But listen to the small word but. Shankara says it turns away an objection, and he states the objection with care. It comes from thinkers in the Mimamsa school, who take the Veda with great seriousness. Their view: the Veda's sentences exist to tell people what to do. So the Upanishads, too, must be about action, perhaps a meditation to perform, or praise of the one who performs it. Shankara answers. The Upanishads, he says, teach Brahman, something that already is, not a task to be done. And then he gives his reason. Anything produced by action has a beginning, and whatever begins also ends. A pot that's made can break. If freedom were the product of an action, it would end too. So freedom, moksha, can't be made. He sorts the results of action: making something new, reaching something, changing something, cleaning something. Freedom, he says, is none of these. It's what the self already is, eternally. What removes the obstacle is knowledge, jnana, the way light doesn't create the room, it shows it. That's why this way is called a path of knowing. Shankara isn't saying actions are pointless; for him, good action and devotion can make the mind ready. But the last step isn't a doing. Some other Vedanta schools see freedom as given by the Lord's grace, met by devotion. Here, Shankara speaks.
screen: `BUT: AN OBJECTION TURNED AWAY.` · `ARE THE UPANISHADS ABOUT ACTION?` · `WHAT BEGINS ALSO ENDS.` · `FREEDOM IS NOT MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop reaching for a minute. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Notice any small effort in the body, a tight jaw, a held belly, a leaning forward. Let each one soften. You don't have to make stillness. Just stop adding effort and see what's already here. If the mind starts working at it, notice that too, and let it go. If you pray, you can rest in whatever you pray to, without asking. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing. On the fourth line, Shankara says freedom isn't produced by any action, so what frees is knowing what already is. Today's word.

Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. Today, catch yourself on tiptoe once, trying to earn something you already have. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, good action and devotion are often understood as preparing the mind, while freedom itself is understood as coming through knowledge of the self.

fork.setup: a Mimamsa thinker says: the Veda tells people what to do, so the Upanishads must be about action too. you're Shankara. what do you answer?
options: agreed: freedom is the reward for the right ritual.
no: they teach what already is, and freedom isn't made.
the Upanishads aren't part of the Veda.
fork.reveal: Shankara says anything made by action ends, so freedom, which is eternal, comes by knowing, not doing.

original.note: Sanskrit: connection, harmony; the key word of Brahma Sutra 1.1.4, the texts fitting together in Brahman.

trapdoor: what you thought: on a path of knowing, you study hard and earn freedom.
what it means: for Shankara, freedom isn't earned or made; knowing removes what hid it.
what a scholar hears: Shankara's long comment on 1.1.4 against the Mimamsa view, and his point that moksha is not produced, reached, changed or purified.
